sections.heading: The House Won't Get Below 80
body: Warm air from the vents, or an outdoor unit that hums and never starts. On a Kansas July afternoon, that's a long wait for an answer.

Wichita summers run an air conditioner hard for months. Heat, dust and cottonwood fluff do the damage: parts that start the motors wear out, fan bearings dry up, and coils clog until the system can't shed heat.

Check three things before you call. Is the thermostat set to cool, and does it have batteries? Is the breaker for the outdoor unit still on? Is the air filter so dirty you can't see through it? A choked filter can freeze the coil and leave you with warm air.
Usually the failure is one part. A weak capacitor makes a unit hum without starting, a worn fan motor stalls, and a refrigerant leak lets the cooling fade a little more every week.
The fix is to replace the part that failed, or to find and repair the leak. A system with years left in it shouldn't be replaced because one piece quit.

sections.heading: The Furnace Clicks but Never Lights
body: Click, click, then nothing, or the vents blow cold when the furnace should be running. A cold snap is when it shows, because that's when the furnace runs all day.

A gas furnace has to light the burners, prove the flame, then start the blower. The igniter wears out from heat cycles, and a sensor coated in soot or dust can shut the whole thing down for safety. Both are small parts.

Check the basics first. Is the thermostat set to heat and above room temperature? Is the furnace switch on, and the breaker too? Is the filter clogged? A starved furnace overheats and shuts itself off.
If those are fine, the usual fix is a new igniter or a cleaned or replaced sensor. We replace the part that failed, and we tell you if what we find is bigger than a part.

sections.heading: Your Furnace Is Old and the Repairs Keep Stacking Up
body: Rooms heat unevenly, the furnace starts and stops, or the shower goes cold halfway through. Old heaters don't fail in one dramatic moment. Parts wear until the repairs look like a down payment on a new one.

Look at the pattern. A furnace that's had a part replaced two winters running is telling you something. So is a water heater tank with rust at the base or sediment rumbling inside it, which is common in hard water.
That's when a new furnace or water heater makes sense, sized for your house and vented right. Nate will tell you when a repair still makes sense and when it doesn't.

sections.heading: One Room Never Gets Comfortable
body: A back bedroom, an addition, a shop. It's hot in July and cold in January, and the thermostat in the hall says everything is fine.
Two things cause it. The main system was never sized for that room, or the ducts leak, kink or run through an unheated space and lose the air on the way.
You can check the easy part yourself. Hold a hand to the vent: weak airflow points to the ducts, and strong airflow that doesn't change the temperature points to a room the system can't keep up with.
We install mini split systems for rooms the main system doesn't reach, and we do ductwork. A mini split heats and cools one room without running new duct to it.

sections.heading: What You Notice, and What It Means
list: **Cold rooms and uneven heat** point to the furnace. A blower that's wearing out, a clogged filter or leaking ducts can cause it, and so can a furnace that can't keep up any more.
**A furnace that starts and stops** is short-cycling. It's often too big for the house, so it heats fast and shuts off, or it's overheating from a dirty filter or a failing part.
**A cold shower halfway through** points to the water heater. Tanks collect sediment, especially in hard water, and sediment covers the bottom of the tank and the heating element or burner.
**Water around the base of the tank** means it's leaking from the inside. A leaking tank can't be repaired.
tail: If you're not sure which unit is the problem, call and tell us what's happening.
body: Wichita houses run a heater hard from November to March, and a cold snap is when a worn one finally quits.
Before you call, check the filter and the thermostat, and look at the base of the water heater for water.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace
body: Replace when the heat exchanger has cracked, because that part can't be fixed safely. Replace when a water heater tank is leaking.
Replace when the unit is old and the repairs are stacking up. A rule of thumb: if a repair costs a big share of a new unit, the money is better spent on the new one.
Repair when one part has failed and the rest of the unit is in decent shape. An igniter, a blower motor or a thermostat can all be swapped without replacing the furnace.
Nate will tell you which one yours is. We also repair what's in your house, so a repair is an answer you can hear from us.

sections.heading: What We Install

**Water heaters,** including heat pump (hybrid) models, which pull heat from the surrounding air to heat the water and cost less to run than a standard electric tank.
**Heat pumps,** for homes that want heating and cooling from one system.
body: The job starts with what's in the house now: where the old unit sits, how it's vented and what it's connected to.

sections.heading: Why the Install Matters
body: A good heater installed badly is still a bad heater. A furnace that's too big short-cycles and wears out early. One that's too small never catches up on a January night.
Sizing comes from the house: its square footage, its insulation, its windows and its ducts. The old unit's size is only a starting point, because the house may have changed since it went in.
Venting is the part people don't see. A gas furnace or water heater has to send combustion gases outside, and a poor connection can put them in the house.
That's why a gas appliance is worth getting installed by someone you can call back. If something smells or sounds wrong afterward, you want to reach the person who set it up.

sections.heading: When You Call About a Part
body: Nate answers. You tell him what the unit is doing, whether it hums, clicks, blows cold or won't start, and he tells you whether it sounds like a part or something bigger.
He explains what he found in plain terms, so you know what broke and what the repair involves. Text works too.

Before you call, check that the thermostat is set right, the breaker is on and the filter is clean. If any of those was the problem, you've saved a visit. If not, you can tell Nate you've checked them.

sections.heading: What You Hear, and Which Part It Is
body: Moving parts wear out first, and the ones that work hardest wear fastest. In Wichita that's a hot summer on the condenser fan and a long winter on the furnace blower.
list: **The unit hums but won't start.** A weak capacitor or contactor, which give a motor its start-up jolt. The motor itself may be fine.
**The outdoor fan or the blower stalls.** The motor bearings have worn. Dust and heat speed that up, and a motor that's been running hot is often the next to go.
**The furnace clicks and quits.** An igniter or a sensor, most often. The igniter cracks after many heat cycles, and a dirty sensor can't prove the flame.
**Cooling slowly fades.** A leak in a refrigerant line or a coil lets refrigerant out. Ice on the lines or a hissing sound is a clue.

image.alt: Ceiling air vent in a quiet Wichita home

tail: The fix is usually to swap the failed part and test the system through a full cycle. A capacitor or contactor is a quick swap. A motor takes longer, because it has to match the unit.
Why replace a motor rather than the unit? A motor is one part in a system built from many. If the compressor, coils and controls are sound, the system has plenty of life left.

sections.heading: A Leak Takes More Than One Visit
body: Topping off refrigerant without finding the leak just starts the clock again. The system runs low, cools badly and strains the compressor, which is the most expensive part to lose.
A slow leak can take more than one visit to chase down. Coils corrode over time, and fittings and joints can weep a little at a time.
Sometimes the part has to be ordered. We explain what failed and what's needed, and we do what we can to keep the system running in the meantime.

sections.heading: Fix the Part or Replace the System
body: A part is the right answer when the rest of the system is in decent shape. It's the wrong answer when the unit is old and failing in several places, or when the compressor or heat exchanger has gone.
Check how many times it's been fixed lately. One part in a long-running system is a repair. A second or third failure in a short span means the system as a whole is wearing out.
Nate will tell you which one you're facing. If replacement makes sense, we install furnaces, water heaters and air conditioners too.

sections.heading: Maintenance That Catches It Early
body: Most parts don't fail without warning. Filters clog, bearings get noisy, coils collect dirt, and the system works harder until something gives.

Cottonwood fluff and yard dust can coat the outdoor coil by midsummer, and a dirty coil makes the system run longer and hotter. A clean filter, a clear space around the outdoor unit and an ear for new noises catch most trouble early.
We do maintenance on heating and cooling equipment, so small problems are found before they become a dead system on the hottest or coldest day of the year.
In winter, the same goes for the furnace: a clean filter, clear vents and a look at the flame. A steady blue flame is what you want to see. Yellow or flickering is worth a call.

items.q: Can the same part fail again?
